question: DreamHouse Realty has an approval process. A manager attempts to approve a record but receives an error. What should a Platform Administrator do to troubleshoot this issue?
optionA: Check if the user in the next approver is inactive or missing.
optionB: Review the page layout to ensure the fields updated in the process are visible.
optionC: Update the field-level security to view on fields that are updated in the process.
optionD: Add a delegated approver for the next approver in the process.
explanation:
Checking whether the user set as the next approver is inactive or missing is the first troubleshooting step. A common cause of errors in an approval process is a breakdown in the approver chain: if an approval step is configured to route to a specific user or a manager who has been deactivated, Salesforce throws an error when the current step tries to advance. The Platform Administrator should check the Next Approver field on the record, or the step definition in Setup, to ensure the target user is active and has a valid Salesforce license. Missing field access typically does not error out the approval engine itself; it only prevents the user from seeing the data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (review the page layout for the updated fields) — field visibility affects what the approver sees, not whether the approval step can advance; a missing field on the layout does not throw an approval error.
Option C (update field-level security on the updated fields) — the same point: FLS governs the user's view of the data, and the approval engine does not fail because a field is hidden.
Option D (add a delegated approver) — a delegated approver is an alternate for a valid approver, not a fix for an inactive or missing one; the step still needs an active target user.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.approvals_troubleshoot.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A user is unable to relate a task to the Course custom object. What should a Platform Administrator do to allow tasks to be related to courses?
optionA: Create a sharing rule for the Course object to grant the user Read/Write access.
optionB: Select Allow Activities on the Course object in Object Manager.
optionC: Add the Open Activities related list to the Course page layout.
optionD: Update the user's profile to grant them Edit access to the Task object.
explanation:
Selecting Allow Activities on the Course object in Object Manager is what lets tasks be related to courses. For a custom object to support Tasks and Events, the Allow Activities setting must be enabled in the object's properties, and when a Platform Administrator creates a custom object this checkbox is often left unchecked by default. Enabling it allows the Related To (WhatId) field on a Task or Event to be linked to records of that custom object type.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (sharing rule granting Read/Write on Course) — sharing rules manage access to existing records; they do not control whether the object is technically capable of having activities associated with it.
Option C (add the Open Activities related list to the layout) — a necessary step for visibility, but it will not work if the underlying Allow Activities feature is not enabled first.
Option D (grant Edit access to Task on the profile) — object permissions on Task govern whether the user can edit tasks at all, not whether a task can be related to a Course record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000385007&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.tracking_activities_for_custom_objects.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Platform Administrator at Cloud Kicks has a custom picklist field on Lead, which is missing on the Contact when leads are converted. Which two steps should the administrator take to ensure these values are populated?
optionA: Update the picklist value with a validation rule.
optionB: Create a custom picklist field on Contact.
optionC: Map the picklist field on the Lead to the Contact.
optionD: Set the picklist field to be required on the Lead object.
explanation:
Creating a custom picklist field on Contact and then mapping the Lead picklist field to it are the two steps. When a Lead is converted into an Account, Contact and Opportunity, standard fields are mapped automatically, but custom fields require manual configuration for data to flow through the conversion. First, the Platform Administrator creates a corresponding custom picklist field on the Contact object with the same values as the Lead field. Second, in the Lead Object Manager under Fields & Relationships, the administrator clicks Map Lead Fields and explicitly maps the Lead custom picklist to the newly created Contact custom picklist. Without this mapping, the data is lost during conversion.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (update the picklist value with a validation rule) — a validation rule ensures data exists on the Lead; it does nothing to transfer that data to the Contact.
Option D (make the picklist required on Lead) — the same point: requiring the field guarantees a value on the Lead, not that the value is carried across at conversion.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.customize_mapleads.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which feature gives a sales team the ability to prioritize deals with recent updates in the List view and Kanban view?
explanation:
Deal Change Highlights is the Lightning Experience feature that helps sales teams quickly identify recent changes to opportunities. In list views and the Kanban view, changes to the Amount or Close Date fields are highlighted with green (for positive changes) or red (for negative changes) arrows and text for seven days. This lets reps and managers visually prioritize deals that have recently shifted in value or timing without opening each record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Big Deal Alerts) — sends an email when an opportunity reaches a set amount or probability; it does not mark recent changes in a list or Kanban view.
Option B (Report Filters) — narrow the rows of a report for general data analysis; they do not highlight field changes in a list view.
Option D (Opportunity Path) — guides users through stages on the record page and does not highlight recent field-level data changes in a list format.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.manage_opportunity_motion.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Platform Administrator at Universal Containers has a screen flow that helps users create new leads. When Lead Source is "Search Engine", the administrator needs to require the user to choose a specific search engine from a picklist. If Lead Source is not "Search Engine", this picklist should be hidden. What is the most efficient way for the administrator to complete this requirement?
optionA: Use a conditional filter in the screen element to only show the Specific Search Engine field only when Lead Source is "Search Engine".
optionB: Use Assignment elements; one for when Lead Source is "Search Engine" and one for everything else.
optionC: Create a picklist for Specific Search Engine, and set conditional visibility so that it is only shown when Lead Source is "Search Engine".
optionD: Configure a picklist for Specific Search Engine, and use a validation rule to conditionally show only when Lead Source is "Search Engine".
explanation:
Creating a picklist for Specific Search Engine and setting conditional visibility so it is only shown when Lead Source is "Search Engine" is the most efficient approach. In Flow Builder, component visibility lets an administrator set logic on individual screen components so they only appear when specific criteria are met: select the Specific Search Engine picklist component within the flow screen and configure its visibility to show only when the Lead Source screen component equals "Search Engine". The form then adapts in real time to the user's input, with no extra screen and no validation error.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a conditional filter in the screen element) — a screen element has no filter; the mechanism that shows or hides a component on a screen is the component's own visibility condition.
Option B (Assignment elements, one per Lead Source case) — assignments set variable values; they cannot show or hide a screen component, and branching this way would need multiple screens and complex logic for something a single visibility rule handles.
Option D (a validation rule to conditionally show the picklist) — validation rules are reactive and only tell the user they made a mistake after they try to save; they cannot show or hide a component, whereas conditional visibility is proactive.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_ref_elements_screen_conditional_visibility.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Platform Administrator at Universal Containers is trying to deactivate a user who has left the company but is unable to do so. What is preventing the administrator from deactivating this user?
optionA: The user is the running user of a dashboard.
optionB: The user is part of an active case assignment rule.
optionC: The user is part of an Opportunity team.
optionD: The user is part of an Account team.
explanation:
The user being part of an active case assignment rule is what blocks the deactivation. Salesforce blocks it outright when the user is still referenced by an active case assignment or escalation rule; the documented error is "You cannot deactivate this user. You cannot deactivate a user who is receiving cases or notifications as part of your case assignment/escalation rules." The fix is to edit the rule entries in Setup and replace the user with an active user or a queue, then deactivate.
Being the running user of a dashboard is not a blocker. Considerations for Deactivating Users lists exactly four things that stop a deactivation - certain system user types, a user selected in a custom hierarchy field, the sole recipient of a workflow email alert, and a Customer Portal Administrator - and a dashboard running user is not among them. What the documentation says about dashboards is milder: when you deactivate a user who owns or runs a dashboard, the dashboard does not return expected results. That is a broken dashboard to clean up afterwards, not a wall in front of the deactivation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (running user of a dashboard) — not in the documented list of deactivation blockers; the dashboard simply stops returning expected results afterwards.
Option C (member of an Opportunity team) — team membership is not a blocker; deactivated users are simply removed from other people's default teams.
Option D (member of an Account team) — the same: account team membership is cleaned up on deactivation, it does not prevent it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000383178&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_deactivate_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: The key pointed at the dashboard running user, which the documentation does not list as a deactivation blocker - it only warns that such a dashboard stops returning expected results. An active case assignment or escalation rule referencing the user does produce a hard error that prevents deactivation, and that is the documented answer. The old explanation had the two options exactly inverted, calling the dashboard a hard system block and saying assignment rules usually permit deactivation.

question: The sales and service teams at Cloud Kicks would like to have more visibility into their pipeline and stay on top of every case. A Platform Administrator needs to quickly create dashboards for each of the teams but does not know where to start. What should the administrator do?
optionA: Use the Salesforce Labs Field Service Dashboards for service teams from AppExchange.
optionB: Enable Einstein Analytics and build custom dashboards using advanced analytics tools.
optionC: Use the Salesforce Labs CRM Dashboards for sales teams from AppExchange.
optionD: Manually create dashboards without using any prebuilt templates or packages.
explanation:
Using the Salesforce Labs CRM Dashboards for sales teams from AppExchange is the right starting point for an administrator who needs to deliver dashboards quickly and does not know where to start. Salesforce Labs provides several free, pre-configured dashboard packages, and the CRM Dashboards package includes standard components for sales pipeline, lead tracking and case management. It is an excellent baseline that can be installed in minutes and then customized to fit Cloud Kicks' needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce Labs Field Service Dashboards) — too narrow: it focuses specifically on Field Service rather than the general sales and service visibility both teams asked for.
Option B (enable Einstein Analytics and build custom dashboards) — a separate, more complex product that requires extra licensing and setup; not a quick start.
Option D (manually create dashboards with no templates) — time-consuming, and exactly what the prebuilt package exists to avoid.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.dashboards_install_sample_appexchange.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Agentforce is escalating cases to the support team, but the support team complains they have no context and have to ask the customer to repeat everything. Which configuration issue is the most likely cause of this issue?
optionA: The support team members are missing the Agentforce User permission set.
optionB: The support team's case page layout is missing the agent history component.
optionC: The agent's instructions are preventing the history and context from being saved.
optionD: The handoff is creating a new case instead of transferring the existing session.
explanation:
The support team's case page layout missing the agent history component is the intended answer, but treat this item as unsettled. The scenario - reps receiving an escalated conversation with no visibility of what the customer already told the AI - is a real Agentforce concern, and the intended reading is that the reps' Case page is not surfacing the preceding conversation, so the transcript exists but is not on screen for them.
Current Salesforce documentation does not name an agent history component, and Transfer Conversations from an Agent with an Omni-Channel Flow describes the Escalation subagent and the outbound Omni-Channel flow without specifying any Case page component that carries the transcript to the rep. Option D - a handoff that opens a new case rather than continuing the existing session - would produce the same symptom and cannot be ruled out from the documentation.
The key is left where the source put it, but the component name in the option is not one you should memorise as Salesforce terminology.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (reps missing the Agentforce User permission set) — that permission set governs a user's own access to Agentforce features; reps receiving an escalated case do not need it to see the conversation, so its absence would not produce this symptom.
Option C (the agent's instructions preventing history from being saved) — agent instructions shape how the agent behaves in the conversation; they do not control whether the session transcript is persisted or shown to a rep.
Option D (the handoff creating a new case instead of transferring the session) — would produce the same symptom and the documentation does not rule it out; it is not the exam's intended answer, which is why the item is flagged rather than moved.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.service_agent_escalation.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: This item could not be settled against documentation. The keyed option names an agent history component that current Agentforce documentation does not describe, and option D would explain the same symptom. The key is unchanged, but do not treat the option wording as official terminology.

question: How should a Platform Administrator view Currencies, Fiscal Year settings, and Business Hours in Salesforce?
explanation:
Company Settings (formerly Company Profile) is the central Setup location where global organizational parameters such as Currencies, Fiscal Year and Business Hours are managed. Under Company Information the admin can view the Org ID, default time zone and primary currency. The Fiscal Year settings define whether the organization follows a standard Gregorian calendar or a custom fiscal cycle. Business Hours define the working times for the organization, which is critical for calculating milestones in Service Cloud or escalation rules. If Multi-Currency is enabled, this is also where exchange rates and active currencies are managed. These settings establish the baseline for how data is interpreted and how time-based automation functions across the entire instance, so getting them right is vital for accurate financial reporting and maintaining service level agreements.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (User Management Settings) — holds user-experience toggles such as enhanced profile and permission set UIs, not fiscal year, currencies or business hours.
Option C (Custom Settings) — a developer feature for storing custom configuration data accessible from Apex and formulas; unrelated to the org's company-level parameters.
Option D (Feature Settings) — groups product-area configuration such as Sales, Service and Chatter features; the company-wide currency and calendar settings are not there.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.setting_the_fiscal_year.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.customize_supporthours.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks uses the standard Account Type field to indicate different account tiers. Users find this confusing, so management has asked that the field be changed to read "Tier" on the page layouts. How should a Platform Administrator implement this change?
optionA: Edit the Type field and change the name.
optionC: Build a custom field called Tier and delete Type.
optionD: Create a global picklist value set.
explanation:
Rename Tabs and Labels is the tool for changing the display name of a standard field such as Account Type globally across the organization. It lets an administrator modify the singular and plural labels for standard objects and the field labels for their standard fields; renaming "Type" to "Tier" is then reflected on page layouts, in report column headers and in list views. It is the preferred method because it preserves the underlying data and logic associated with the standard field.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (edit the Type field and change the name) — standard field names cannot be edited in the Fields & Relationships menu; the label of a standard field is only changeable through Rename Tabs and Labels.
Option C (build a custom Tier field and delete Type) — a destructive and complex process that would require data migration and could break existing reports or integrations.
Option D (create a global picklist value set) — governs the values a picklist offers, not the label of the field itself.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.customize_rename.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Platform Administrator at Cloud Kicks needs to temporarily remove one dashboard from a shared folder with several dashboards to make some required changes. How should the administrator achieve this?
optionA: Remove View access to the shared folder.
optionB: Edit the dashboard properties and move it to a private dashboards folder.
optionC: Remove the permission set to the dashboard from the users.
optionD: Create a private group and add the dashboard to it.
explanation:
Editing the dashboard properties and moving it to a private dashboards folder is how to temporarily remove one dashboard from a shared folder. Access to reports and dashboards is determined by the folder they are stored in: if a dashboard is in a shared folder, anyone with access to that folder can view it. Moving just this dashboard to a private folder (such as My Private Dashboards) takes it out of public view without affecting the rest of the folder's contents; once moved, only the administrator (and those with View All Data) can see it while the changes are being made.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (remove View access to the shared folder) — would hide all the dashboards in that folder, not just the one being changed.
Option C (remove the permission set to the dashboard from the users) — permission sets control functional access such as the ability to create or edit dashboards, not the visibility of an individual dashboard.
Option D (create a private group and add the dashboard to it) — groups are for Chatter collaboration and for folder sharing targets; a dashboard cannot be added to a group, and folder membership is what governs its visibility.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.access_dashboard_folders.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A user at Northern Trail Outfitters is having trouble logging in to Salesforce. The user's login history shows that this person has attempted to log in multiple times and has been locked out of the organization. Which two steps should a Platform Administrator take to help the user log in to Salesforce?
optionA: Log in as the user to unlock the user and reset the password.
optionB: Use the unlock button on the user's record detail page.
optionC: Reset password on the user's record detail page.
optionD: Reset the password policies to allow the user to login.
explanation:
Using the Unlock button on the user's record detail page and resetting the password from the same page are the two steps. When a user is locked out due to too many incorrect login attempts, the Platform Administrator first clicks Unlock, which clears the lockout status immediately. Second, because the user likely forgot their credentials (which caused the failed attempts), the administrator uses Reset Password, which sends a link to the user's email so they can create a new password and log in successfully.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (log in as the user to unlock and reset the password) — Login As is a troubleshooting tool for seeing what the user sees; it cannot bypass a lockout or change a password on the user's behalf.
Option D (reset the password policies) — changing password policies affects the entire organization and is not a valid way to help a single locked-out individual.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_unlock.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: At Cloud Kicks, cases are being assigned a default Case Owner and showing a Created By and Last Modified By that is not expected. The company wants to change this to an integration user to alleviate confusion with the business. What should a Platform Administrator edit to change this in Salesforce?
explanation:
Support Settings is the configuration page to edit. It is where a Platform Administrator defines the Default Case Owner and the Automated Case User. The Automated Case User is the user listed in the case history for automated actions such as those triggered by assignment rules, escalation rules or Email-to-Case, so an unexpected name in Created By or Last Modified By during these automated processes usually means this setting points to a specific administrator or system user. Updating the Automated Case User to a dedicated integration user ensures the audit trail clearly distinguishes manual edits by staff from automated updates by the system.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Process Automation Settings) — governs flow and process-automation behaviour such as the default workflow user; it does not set the default case owner or automated case user.
Option B (Debug Logs) — a diagnostic tool for capturing execution logs; it changes nothing about how cases are owned or stamped.
Option C (Support Processes) — define which case status values each record type can use; they do not set the default owner or the automated case user.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.customize_supportrules.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A group of sales reps can view each other's orders on a report; however, they would like a report to view just their own orders. What should a Platform Administrator do to set up a report for the sales reps?
optionA: Set the Opportunity Filter for Primary as True.
optionC: Set Organization Wide Defaults of Order object to Private.
optionD: Save the report in a private folder for the user.
explanation:
Filtering by Opportunity Owner equals $USER is the answer, because Salesforce reports support a single filter that personalises itself per viewer. Set a filter on a user field - Owner, Opportunity Owner, Created By - and choose the relative value option; the filter value then resolves to the currently signed-in user, so one saved report shows each rep only their own records. Create Personalized Report Filters documents this and notes it is supported only for user-related fields such as Username and Owner fields. Building a separate report per rep does not scale.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (set the Opportunity Filter for Primary as True) — the primary filter on an order report selects orders flagged as primary; it has nothing to do with who owns them.
Option C (set the Order object's OWD to Private) — would restrict visibility generally, but the reps are supposed to keep seeing each other's records; they only want this one report scoped to themselves, which is a reporting concern, not a sharing concern.
Option D (save the report in a private folder for the user) — hides the report from everyone else rather than filtering its rows, and would need a copy per rep.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=release-notes.rn_rd_reports_relative_value_filter.htm&language=en_US&release=242&type=5

question: A salesperson complains that the Log a Call button is missing from the highlights panel of an Opportunity page. What is the reason for this?
optionA: The Log a Call action will appear within the Activity Component as a standard behavior rather than the highlights panel.
optionB: The Log a Call action has not been added to the Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions section of the page layout.
optionC: The custom Log a Call permission is missing from the user's profile and assigned permission sets.
optionD: The custom Log a Call permission has been disabled at the org level in Setup.
explanation:
The Log a Call action not having been added to the Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions section of the page layout is the reason. In Lightning Experience, the buttons and actions that appear in the highlights panel of a record are controlled by that section of the page layout, so if Log a Call is missing it is usually because it has not been dragged into that section in the page layout editor.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Log a Call appears in the Activity component instead, by standard behaviour) — standard actions can appear in the Activity component, but their presence in the header is explicitly configured through the page layout; the component does not replace the highlights panel.
Option C (the custom Log a Call permission is missing from the profile) — there is no specific Log a Call permission that would hide only that button; a user who can create Tasks can use Log a Call if it is on the layout.
Option D (the custom Log a Call permission is disabled at the org level) — the same: no such org-level permission exists.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.adding_actions_using_ple.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a private sharing model for Opportunities and uses Opportunity teams. Criteria- based sharing rules are not used. A sales rep at UC leaves the company, and their user record is deactivated. The rep is later rehired in the same role. A Platform Administrator activates the old user record. The user is added to the same default Opportunity teams but is no longer able to see the same records the user worked on before leaving the company. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The stage of the opportunity records was changed to Closed Lost.
optionB: The record type of the opportunity records was changed.
optionC: The records were manually shared with the user.
optionD: Permission sets were removed when the user was deactivated.
explanation:
The records having been manually shared with the user is the likely cause. Salesforce has managed sharing (role hierarchy, sharing rules) and manual sharing, and a critical platform behaviour is that when a user is deactivated, all their manual shares (records shared with them by other users using the Share button) are automatically and permanently deleted. Even if the user record is reactivated later, those manual shares do not return. Because UC uses a Private model and no criteria-based sharing rules, the user's previous access relied on those one-off shares; reactivating and re-adding them to teams grants new access, but the historical manual shares are gone.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the opportunities were changed to Closed Lost) — the stage of a record does not change who can see it under a private model; a closed opportunity is as visible to its sharers as an open one.
Option B (the record type was changed) — record types control picklists and layouts, not record-level visibility; changing one does not remove access.
Option D (permission sets were removed on deactivation) — permission sets control what a user can do, not which specific records they can see in a private sharing model, and deactivation does not strip them.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_deactivate_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.granting_access_to_records_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Ursa Major Solar wants to assist users with a guided expense report process to simplify submissions, routing, and authorizations. Which two tools should a Platform Administrator use to build this solution?
explanation:
Flow Builder and an Approval Process are the two tools. Flow Builder creates the user-facing interface (a screen flow) that guides the employee through the expense report submission, ensuring all necessary data is collected in a structured way and replacing a static page layout with a step-by-step wizard. Once the record is created, the flow can submit it into an Approval Process, which handles the routing and authorizations by sending the report to the appropriate manager or director for sign-off. Together they provide an end-to-end automation for a guided, routed, authorized process.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Validation Rule) — only prevents errors on save; it neither guides users through steps nor routes records for approval.
Option B (Quick Action) — can launch a flow, but it is an entry point rather than the logic engine that guides submission or handles routing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.what_are_approvals.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_forms_with_screen_flow_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: At Cloud Kicks, when a rep needs to seek additional support help, there's a series of actions the company wants to ensure are taken. The steps include sending an email and changing the status and owner of the case. What should a Platform Administrator use to give the reps an easy way to make these updates?
explanation:
Macros with Quick Actions give reps an easy way to perform this repetitive sequence. A macro lets a user perform multiple steps - changing a case status, reassigning the case owner and sending a pre-written email - with a single click; combined with quick actions, macros navigate the user interface, populate fields and submit the changes automatically. That reduces manual data entry and ensures the company's required support process is followed consistently, while leaving the rep in control of when to trigger it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Case Assignment Rules) — fully automated and run on save; they assign owners but do not send a chosen email or set a status at the rep's request.
Option C (Quick Text with Email Templates) — assists with typing the email but does not automate field changes or ownership transfers.
Option D (Autolaunched Flows with Email Alerts) — fully automated and triggered on save, which is not appropriate when the rep needs to decide when to seek support help; the ask is a one-click rep-initiated action.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.macros_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Users at Cloud Kicks want to see information that is more useful for their role on the Case page. How should a Platform Administrator make the pages more dynamic and easier to use?
optionA: Add component visibility filters to the components.
optionB: Include more tab components with filters.
optionC: Remove fields from the record details component.
optionD: Delete the extra components from the page.
explanation:
Adding component visibility filters to the components is how to make the Case page more dynamic. In the Lightning App Builder, component visibility filters show or hide parts of a record page based on criteria such as the user's profile, a field value or the record type. For example, a Financial Details component can appear only when the viewing user has the Finance User profile, or a Recall Instructions component can be hidden unless Case Reason is Product Defect. That prevents information overload by ensuring users only see the tools and data relevant to their role or to the current state of the record, and it personalises the page without maintaining several copies of it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (more tab components with filters) — adds more places to look rather than fewer; tabs do not adapt to the user's role, so every user still sees everything.
Option C (remove fields from the record details component) — affects all users equally, so it cannot give each role the information that is useful to it.
Option D (delete the extra components) — the same: a blanket removal for everyone, failing to provide role-specific utility.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_components_visibility.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Object Manager and Lightning App Builder

question: Marketing users at Cloud Kicks have been completing the Lead Source field inconsistently, with values like Web, Website, and Online. To ensure data quality, a Platform Administrator needs to standardize these records. Which Flow should the administrator use to clean up these inconsistent Lead Source values?
explanation:
A schedule-triggered flow is the right tool for cleaning up data that is already in the org. It runs on a schedule you set - once, or daily, or weekly - and processes every record matching its criteria, so it can sweep the whole Lead table, find the Lead Source values that read Website or Online, and rewrite them to the standard Web.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Segment triggered flow) — there is no such thing as a segment-triggered flow in Flow Builder.
Option B (Record triggered flow) — only fires when a record is created or updated, so it would fix new bad values going forward but would never touch the historical records that are the actual problem here.
Option D (Screen flow) — needs a person to run it record by record; it cannot sweep the existing data.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_concepts_trigger_schedule.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks is concerned that not everyone on the sales team is entering key data into accounts and opportunities that they own. Also, the team is concerned that if the key information changes, it does not get updated in Salesforce. A Platform Administrator wants to get a better understanding of their data quality and record completeness. What should the administrator do to accomplish this?
optionA: Explore AppExchange for data quality and record completeness solutions.
optionB: Create a report for Accounts and Opportunities highlighting missing data.
optionC: Subscribe the sales reps to a monthly report for accounts and opportunities.
optionD: Configure the key fields as required fields on the page layout.
explanation:
Creating a report for Accounts and Opportunities highlighting missing data is what gives the administrator a better understanding of current data quality and record completeness. Reports (or dashboards) that surface blank or missing key fields - using filters like "Field equals (blank)" or formula fields that flag incompleteness - directly assess the existing data by showing which records lack required information. Salesforce's data quality guidance emphasises using reports and dashboards (for example the Account, Contact & Opportunity Data Quality Dashboard) to identify missing fields and measure completeness before implementing fixes: assess first through reporting, then enforce improvements.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (explore AppExchange for data quality solutions) — useful for advanced or ongoing solutions, but it skips the initial assessment step the administrator is asking for.
Option C (subscribe the reps to a monthly report) — helps with awareness among reps but does not give the administrator an overview of data quality.
Option D (make the key fields required on the layout) — prevents future gaps but reveals nothing about the current missing data or outdated records.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/data_quality

question: A Platform Administrator needs to configure an approval process for the sales team when opportunities that meet particular conditions are closed. How should the administrator make sure the right records are included in the process?
optionB: Use Dynamic Forms to display a button.
optionD: Add a validation rule to the opportunity.
explanation:
Adding specific entry criteria is the fundamental way to control which records enter an approval process. During setup of the process the administrator specifies field-level conditions (for example Amount > 50,000 AND Stage = Closed Won) that a record must meet to be eligible; if a user attempts to submit a record that does not meet them, Salesforce displays an error and prevents the process from starting. That ensures the finance or management teams are only notified of deals that actually require their sign-off.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Dynamic Forms to display a button) — can show or hide the Submit for Approval button, but it does not enforce the underlying business logic of which records the process accepts.
Option C (create a screen flow) — a flow could launch the submission, but the entry criteria inside the approval process itself are the gatekeeper for which records are included.
Option D (add a validation rule) — prevents bad data on save; it does not route records for approval or decide which ones qualify.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.approvals_create_entrycriteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Platform Administrator for Cloud Kicks needs to ensure that only the financial records belonging to each individual user are visible on the report, in order to meet scope of the data privacy requirements. How should the administrator achieve this?
optionA: Set sharing model as Public Read/Write for the respective object(s).
optionB: Set sharing model as Private for the respective object(s).
optionC: Create multiple reports, each filtered to show records owned by each user.
optionD: Use Apex sharing to hide records.
explanation:
Setting the sharing model to Private for the respective object(s) is the answer, because the organization-wide default is the foundation of Salesforce record security. When an object's OWD is Private, a user can only see the records they own (plus those below them in the role hierarchy), and when that user runs a report the report engine automatically respects those sharing settings and displays only the records the user is authorised to see. One report then serves everyone, scoped correctly per viewer.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Public Read/Write) — would let everyone see everything, the opposite of the privacy requirement.
Option C (multiple reports, one filtered per user) — neither secure nor scalable; the records remain visible to anyone who edits a filter or runs a different report.
Option D (Apex sharing to hide records) — a complex coding solution that is unnecessary when the standard Private sharing model meets the requirement through simple configuration.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to ensure that cases are routed to the right people at the right time, but there is a growing support organization. The business wants to be able to move people around and adjust the work they get without having to request extra assistance or rely on the administrator teams. Which tool allows the business to control its own assignment of work?
explanation:
Omni-Channel is the tool that lets the business control its own assignment of work. It routes work items (cases, leads or custom objects) to the most available and qualified agents in real time, and its management is dynamic: through queues and presence statuses a support manager or supervisor can monitor agent workloads, adjust capacity or move people between service channels without modifying system configuration or involving the Platform Administrator. It supports routing models such as Least Active and Most Available so work is distributed fairly, and supervisors can see who is logged in and what they are working on, allowing immediate adjustments to handle spikes in case volume.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Case Assignment Rules) — static rule logic that an administrator maintains in Setup; moving people or changing what they get means editing the rules, which is exactly the dependency the business wants to remove.
Option B (Email-to-Case) — an intake channel that creates cases from email; it does not route or balance work among agents.
Option D (Lead Assignment Rules) — the same static mechanism as case assignment rules, and for leads rather than the support cases in question.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.omnichannel_intro.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks wants to ensure that every client has support based on the level of service that has been agreed on in the sales cycle. There are tiers to this support model, Gold, Silver, and Bronze. What should a Platform Administrator create to ensure that this is part of every client's account once they become a client?
optionC: Email to Case for each service level
optionD: Case Assignment Rules for each client
explanation:
A flow to assign Entitlements is what ensures the agreed service level is part of every client's account. Salesforce manages support tiers such as Gold, Silver and Bronze through Entitlement Management, where an entitlement defines the specific type of support a customer is eligible for. A record-triggered flow can run whenever an account is updated to Customer status or a Service Level field is populated, and automatically create or link the matching entitlement record to that account, so when a new case is opened the agent immediately sees the SLA associated with that customer.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Routing Configuration for each client) — routing configurations decide which agents receive work in Omni-Channel; they do not define the level of service a client is owed.
Option C (Email to Case for each service level) — an intake method for creating cases from email, not a service-level tracking tool.
Option D (Case Assignment Rules for each client) — decide who gets the case, not what support tier applies to it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.entitlements_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Ursa Major Solar has its business hours set from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM for the reps that are on Pacific Time. The reps on Eastern Time need business hours set to start 3 hours earlier to cover for support. How should a Platform Administrator solve for this issue?
optionA: Adjust the current business hours to accommodate the Eastern time zone.
optionB: Allow the reps to set business hours manually.
optionC: Set temporary business hours for each time zone.
optionD: Create one set of business hours per time zone.
explanation:
Creating one set of business hours per time zone is the solution. Salesforce allows multiple Business Hours records to support teams in different time zones, so the Platform Administrator creates two distinct sets - one for Pacific support (9 AM to 5 PM PT) and one for Eastern support (9 AM to 5 PM ET). This matters because business hours drive escalation rules and milestones: an escalation on an Eastern-based case should start counting at 9 AM ET, not 9 AM PT. One set per time zone keeps the support team's performance metrics and automated routing accurate and localised.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (adjust the current business hours to cover both) — would produce a 12-hour window that does not accurately reflect either team's true availability.
Option B (let reps set business hours manually) — users cannot set their own business hours in a way that affects system automation; business hours are an org-level Setup record.
Option C (temporary business hours per time zone) — the requirement is ongoing coverage, not a temporary override, and business hours have no temporary mode; the answer is a permanent record per zone.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.customize_supporthours.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which two data loss considerations should a Platform Administrator keep in mind when changing a custom field type from Text to Picklist?
optionA: Auto updates will be made to Visualforce references to prevent data loss.
optionB: Any list view based on the custom field is deleted.
optionC: There will be no data loss with use of a global value set.
optionD: Assignment and escalation rules may be affected.
explanation:
Any list view based on the field being deleted, and assignment and escalation rules possibly being affected, are the two data loss considerations when changing a custom field from Text to Picklist. List views that use the field as a filter are automatically deleted (or the filter removed) because the filter logic for a text field (operators like contains) differs fundamentally from a picklist (equals). Assignment rules, escalation rules and validation rules that reference the field may be disabled or function incorrectly, because those automations rely on specific text strings; changing the field to a picklist requires the administrator to review and update the logic to align with the new picklist values.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Visualforce references auto-updated) — Salesforce does not automatically update code references; the administrator must review them.
Option C (no data loss with a global value set) — data loss can still occur if existing text values do not exactly match the new picklist entries, whether or not those entries come from a global value set.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.notes_on_changing_custom_field_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) customers have provided feedback that their support cases are not being responded to quickly enough. UC wants to send all unassigned cases that have been open for more than 2 hours to an urgent Case queue and alert the support manager. Which feature should a Platform Administrator configure to meet this requirement?
explanation:
Case Escalation Rules are designed to automate actions when a case has remained in a certain state for a defined period of time. The requirement has two time-based triggers - move the case after 2 hours and alert a manager - and escalation rules let the administrator define escalation actions that execute when the time threshold is reached, such as Reassign to Queue and Notify Manager.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Case Scheduled Reports) — provide information on a schedule but do not move records or perform automated reassignments.
Option B (Case Dashboard Refreshes) — the same: a refreshed dashboard shows the backlog, it does not act on it.
Option D (Case Assignment Rules) — only fire when a case is first created or when manually triggered, not after a time delay.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.rules_escalation_actions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A sales manager at DreamHouse Realty wants sales users to have a quick way to view and update the opportunities in their pipeline expected to close in the next 90 days. What should a Platform Administrator do to accomplish this request?
optionA: Create a custom report and schedule the sales users to receive it each day as a reminder to update their opportunities.
optionB: Make a new Sales dashboard and add a component that shows all opportunities that meet the criteria.
optionC: Enable Sales Console and show users how to open a tab for each opportunity in the pipeline that meets the requirements.
optionD: Create a list view on the Opportunity object and recommend users switch the view to Kanban to edit by drag and drop.
explanation:
Creating a list view on the Opportunity object and recommending users switch it to Kanban to edit by drag and drop gives both the quick view and the quick update. The Platform Administrator creates a public list view filtered on Close Date equals NEXT 90 DAYS; switched to the Kanban display, it shows the reps' deals organised by stage, dragging a card changes the Stage field automatically, and the side panel edits other key fields. Kanban is the native productivity feature built for pipeline management.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a scheduled custom report as a daily reminder) — good for visibility, but a report is read-only; it is not optimised for the rapid record updates the manager is asking for.
Option B (a Sales dashboard component) — a visualisation, not an editing surface; users still have to open each record to update it.
Option C (Sales Console with a tab per opportunity) — opening a tab for every pipeline record is the slow path, not a quick way to view and update them together.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.kanban_use.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks has three teams of customer service reps that use a custom field on the Case object to populate the team assigned to manage the tickets. The customer support manager would like a Custom Dashboard to show data specific to each team. What should a Platform Administrator do to meet this requirement?
optionA: Create separate Dashboards for each Customer Support team.
optionB: Create a Dashboard with widgets specific to each team.
optionC: Create a Dashboard that uses Dashboard filters to show specific team data.
optionD: Add Cross Filters to switch between the three customer service teams.
explanation:
Creating a dashboard that uses dashboard filters to show specific team data is the answer, because it avoids the burden of building and maintaining multiple identical dashboards. Adding a filter on the Team Assigned custom field produces a single dashboard the manager can toggle between Team A, Team B and Team C; each time a filter value is selected, every component that uses that field (or a mapped equivalent) refreshes to show only that team's data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (separate dashboards per team) — inefficient and leads to dashboard sprawl, with three copies to keep in step.
Option B (one dashboard with widgets specific to each team) — a cluttered and confusing interface, and each change to the layout has to be made three times.
Option D (Cross Filters to switch between teams) — cross filters are a report feature that filters records by their relationship to other objects; they are not a dashboard-level viewing control.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.dashboard_filters_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The Cloud Kicks CFO requires any opportunity over $100,000 to be automatically sent to them, so they can sign off on the record before the deal closes. Which feature should a Platform Administrator use to fulfill this requirement?
explanation:
Flow Approvals are the feature to use. The requirement has two halves: a record has to enter a review because it crosses a threshold, and it has to get there without anyone clicking anything. Approvals are the review mechanism, and Flow is what makes the submission automatic.
Flow Approval Processes are the current form of this. They can be built as record-triggered, so an opportunity crossing 100,000 dollars is submitted for the CFO's sign-off the moment it is saved. The older equivalent is a record-triggered flow that calls the Submit for Approval action against a classic approval process; either way, the automation is what removes the manual step.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Submit for Approval button) — the manual path the requirement rules out; it needs a user to press it.
Option B (Einstein Next Best Action) — recommends actions to users; it does not route records for authorisation.
Option C (Apex Triggers) — could be made to work, but they are code where a declarative tool already covers the case.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.automate_automated_approvals.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters wants to initiate expense reports from Salesforce to the external HR system. Managers and directors need to review this process. Which two tools should a Platform Administrator configure?
explanation:
An Outbound Message and an Approval Process are the two tools. The Approval Process handles the internal workflow, ensuring the manager and director sign off on the expense report; once the final approval is granted, an approval action fires, and the administrator uses an Outbound Message as that action. Outbound messages send specific record data (XML via API) to an external URL whenever a record change occurs, which is a reliable, declarative way to hand the report to the HR system.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Email Alert Action) — sends a notification email; it does not transfer record data to an external system.
Option C (Quick Action) — a user-facing shortcut for creating or updating records; it supports neither the review workflow nor the external data transfer.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.what_are_approvals.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Ursa Major Solar wants to roll out the Salesforce mobile app, and the first information it wants its users to see is the Top Opportunities report. What should a Platform Administrator configure to achieve this?
optionA: Add the Reports tab to the Salesforce mobile app.
optionB: Enable Today for the Salesforce mobile app.
optionC: Enable Mobile Home for the Salesforce mobile app.
optionD: Add the Dashboards tab to the Salesforce mobile app.
explanation:
Enabling Mobile Home for the Salesforce mobile app is what puts the Top Opportunities report first. Mobile Home is a customizable landing page that acts as the default start page for users; administrators add cards such as reports, pinned records and upcoming events, so a Report card for Top Opportunities can be placed at the very top of the screen and be the first thing users see on opening the app.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (add the Reports tab) — lets users find the report, but does not present its data on the home screen.
Option B (enable Today) — Today focuses on calendar events and tasks rather than customised report data.
Option D (add the Dashboards tab) — the same as the Reports tab: navigable, but not what users see first.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.salesforce_app_mobile_home.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Platform Administrator at Universal Containers is asked to restrict login access for users to specific hours and specific IP addresses to help minimize the risk of bad actors getting into the org. Which setting should the administrator update to accomplish this?
explanation:
The user's profile is the setting to update, because security restrictions like Login Hours and Login IP Ranges are managed at the profile level. Once configured on a profile they are strictly enforced: a user who attempts to log in outside the allowed hours or from an unauthorised IP address is denied access entirely, which is one of the most robust ways to secure an org against unauthorised access.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Company Settings) — can set Trusted IP Ranges for the whole org, but those only bypass multi-factor authentication or identity verification; they do not restrict login, and they carry no hours.
Option B (the user's role) — roles control record visibility through the hierarchy, not system access.
Option D (custom permission sets) — permission sets grant many permissions, but Login Hours and Login IP Ranges remain a core profile-level security setting.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.login_hours.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.login_ip_ranges.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks has a custom object called Shipments. The company wants to see all the shipment items from an Account page. When an Account is deleted, the shipments should remain. Which type of relationship should a Platform Administrator make between Shipments and Accounts?
optionA: Accounts should have a lookup to Shipments.
optionB: Shipments should have a master detail to Accounts.
optionC: Shipments should have a lookup to Account.
optionD: Accounts should have a master detail to Shipments.
explanation:
Shipments having a lookup to Account is the right relationship. When child records must persist even if the parent is deleted, a lookup relationship is the correct choice: the Shipment object carries a lookup field pointing to the Account, the shipments show in a related list on the Account page, and when the Account is deleted the shipment records remain (with the lookup cleared or left as is). That keeps historical shipment tracking intact.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Accounts have a lookup to Shipments) — the relationship field always lives on the child or many side (Shipments) pointing to the parent (Account); a lookup on Account would relate one account to one shipment, not show all of an account's shipments.
Option B (Shipments have a master-detail to Accounts) — master-detail cascade-deletes the child records when the master is deleted, so the shipments would not remain.
Option D (Accounts have a master-detail to Shipments) — backwards for the same reason as A, and master-detail would also delete records on the wrong side.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.overview_of_custom_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks' management team is hoping to increase user productivity by switching to consoles instead of the current traditional Salesforce user interface. What should a Platform Administrator use to implement this request?
explanation:
App Manager is what the Platform Administrator uses to move users to a console. The App Manager in Setup is where all Lightning apps are created, edited and assigned to user profiles; within it the admin creates a new app and selects Console Navigation as the navigation style. Console apps let users work on multiple records simultaneously in a workspace-tab layout, which is highly effective for productivity in fast-paced sales or support environments.

Option A (App Builder) — the Lightning App Builder designs the pages within an app; the app's overall structure and navigation style are defined in the App Manager.
Option B (Screen Flow) — a guided user interface that can be used inside a console, but it does not create the console app.

question: Sales reps at Ursa Major Solar are having difficulty managing deals. The leadership team has asked a Platform Administrator to help sales reps prioritize and close more deals. What should the administrator configure to help with these issues?
explanation:
Einstein Opportunity Scoring is the tool that helps sales reps prioritise their pipeline and identify which deals are most likely to close. Part of Salesforce's AI suite, it uses machine learning over past won and lost opportunities to assign a score from 1 to 99 to every open deal, accompanied by key factors - positive and negative - that explain the score (for example "The deal has progressed quickly through stages" or "The close date has been pushed three times"). Reps can then focus on high-scoring deals or take corrective action on low-scoring ones.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Einstein Search Personalization) — improves search results for the user; it does not assist in deal management strategy.
Option B (Einstein Lead Scoring) — scores new prospects at intake; it says nothing about existing deals.
Option D (Einstein Activity Capture) — automates the logging of emails and events but provides no prioritisation logic.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.einstein_sales_opportunity_scoring.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: One of the sales managers at Universal Containers will be going on leave for several months. The executives want to make sure the sales manager does not log in to Salesforce while on leave. What should a Platform Administrator do to ensure the user is not able to log in while on leave?
optionA: Reassign the user's license during leave.
optionB: Change the Login Hours for the profile.
optionD: Restrict Login IP Addresses for the profile.
explanation:
Freezing the user's account is the best practice when a user must be temporarily prevented from logging in while their records, role and historical data stay intact. Freezing stops access immediately without deactivating the user - deactivation can be problematic if the user is the running user for dashboards or is part of active hierarchy logic - and it is a one-click action on the user record, targeted at one individual and easily reversed when the manager returns.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (reassign the user's license during leave) — would require deactivating the user first, with all the side effects freezing avoids.
Option B (change the profile's Login Hours) — profile settings affect every user assigned to that profile, not just the manager on leave.
Option D (restrict Login IP Addresses on the profile) — the same profile-wide blast radius, and an IP restriction does not stop a login from an allowed network anyway.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_freeze.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Ursa Major Solar (UMS) wants a place within Salesforce to discuss sensitive records. UMS would like to be able to add new members but does not want non-members to be able to see any information about the forum. What should a Platform Administrator configure to achieve this?
explanation:
A Chatter Unlisted Group is the right configuration when even the existence of the group must be hidden from non-members. An unlisted group does not appear in search results or group lists and requires an explicit invitation to join, so only members know the forum exists - the highest privacy setting available. Unlisted groups must be enabled in Chatter Settings before administrators can create them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Chatter Private Group) — hides the content, but the group itself still appears in searches and lists, so non-members can see that it exists.
Option C (Chatter Public Group) — visible and joinable by everyone; unsuitable for sensitive discussions.
Option D (Private Chatter Channel) — not a Chatter collaboration feature; the term does not describe a group type in Salesforce.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.collab_unlisted_groups_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What are three characteristics of a master-detail relationship?
optionA: Each object can have up to five master-detail relationships.
optionB: Permissions for the detail record are set independently of the master.
optionC: Roll-up summaries are supported in master-detail relationships.
optionD: The master object can be a standard or custom object.
optionE: The owner field on the detail records is the owner of the master record.
explanation:
Roll-up summaries being supported, the master object being standard or custom, and the detail records taking the master's owner are the three documented traits of a master-detail relationship. Roll-up summary fields only exist on the master side of a master-detail relationship - that is the one relationship type that lets a parent count, sum, or take the minimum or maximum of a field on its children. The master can be a standard object or a custom object; the detail side is always custom. And the detail record has no owner of its own: ownership and record-level sharing are inherited from the master.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (up to five master-detail relationships per object) — wrong on the number: an object can have at most two master-detail relationships.
Option B (detail permissions set independently of the master) — the opposite of how it works: permissions on a detail record are derived from the master, which is what makes the relationship tight rather than loose.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.relationships_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_about_roll_up_summary_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A sales rep has a list of 300 accounts with contacts that they want to load at one time. Which tool should a Platform Administrator utilize to import the records to Salesforce?
explanation:
The Data Import Wizard is the ideal tool for importing a relatively small number of records (up to 50,000) involving standard objects like Accounts and Contacts together. One of its unique strengths is handling an Account and Contact import in a single pass, automatically linking contacts to the correct accounts based on name or site. For 300 records it offers a simple browser-based interface with built-in duplicate checking, which is the most user-friendly and efficient choice for this request.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Dataloader.io) — a third-party cloud loader that can handle 300 records, but it is reserved for larger or more complex loads and adds setup a 300-row job does not need.
Option B (Manual Import) — entering 300 accounts and their contacts by hand is not a load tool at all.
Option D (Data Loader) — built for much larger datasets (up to 5 million records) and more complex objects; it lacks the wizard's one-pass account-and-contact linking and duplicate checking.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.faq_data_import_wizard_what_kind_objects.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks needs to be able to show different picklist values for sales and marketing users. Which two options meet this requirement?
optionA: Two permission sets, one record type, one picklist
optionB: One record type, two profiles, one picklist
optionC: One page layout, two record types, one picklist
optionD: Two page layouts, one record type, two picklists
explanation:
One page layout with two record types and one picklist, and two page layouts with one record type and two picklists, are the two options that show different picklist values to sales and marketing users. The first, and most common, uses record types: a single picklist field can have its available values filtered per record type, so a Sales record type and a Marketing record type each expose their own subset, and the record types are assigned to the respective users' profiles. The second uses two separate picklist fields (for example Sales Category and Marketing Category), placing only the relevant field on the page layout assigned to each team - less common, but effective if the data needs to be stored in entirely different buckets.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (two permission sets, one record type, one picklist) — permission sets grant permissions and record-type access; they do not filter the values a picklist offers, and with one record type there is nothing to filter by.
Option B (one record type, two profiles, one picklist) — profiles do not filter picklist values; they only control which record types a user can access, and with a single record type both profiles see the same values.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.editing_picklists_for_record_types_and_business_processes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Sales reps miss key fields when filling out an opportunity record through the sales process. Reps need to move forward in stages but are unable to enter a previous stage. Which three options should a Platform Administrator use to address this need?
optionA: Mark fields required on the page layout.
optionB: Use Flow to mark fields required.
explanation:
Marking fields required on the page layout, configuring Opportunity Path, and using validation rules are the three options. Opportunity Path gives a visual representation of the stages and lets the admin highlight Key Fields and Guidance for Success for each stage, making clear what information is needed to progress. Validation rules enforce it, preventing a move to the next stage if specific fields are blank (for example AND(ISCHANGED(StageName), ISBLANK(Discovery_Notes__c))). Required fields on the page layout ensure the most fundamental data points are always captured. Together they provide a robust framework for managing the sales lifecycle.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (use Flow to mark fields required) — Flow can do many things, but it is not the way to mark a field required in the record UI; that is a page layout, field definition or validation rule concern.
Option E (enable guided selling) — Guided Selling is a Salesforce CPQ term for product recommendation, not a feature of standard opportunity stage management.

question: Management at Universal Containers would like to share dashboard components with their team in Chatter but currently does not have access to this capability. How should a Platform Administrator make this functionality available to management?
optionB: Select Download Chart on the component.
optionC: Set View Dashboard As to the dashboard viewer.
explanation:
Enabling dashboard feed tracking is what makes sharing dashboard components in Chatter available. Chatter feed tracking lets changes to records and interactions be tracked and shared in the feed; for dashboards specifically, enabling it lets users follow a dashboard and use Post to Feed on individual dashboard components, so management can call out successes or concerns by tagging team members in a post that includes the visual chart.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (enable reporting snapshots) — reporting snapshots are for historical trend reporting, not social sharing.
Option B (Download Chart on the component) — a manual file-handling step rather than an integrated Chatter feature.
Option C (set View Dashboard As to the viewer) — determines whose data visibility the dashboard runs with; it does not control Chatter functionality.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.dashboards_post_to_dashboard_feed.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks wants a report to categorize accounts into small, medium, and large based on the dollar value found in the Contract Value field. Which feature should a Platform Administrator use to meet this request?
explanation:
A Bucket Column is the most efficient way to categorise records in a report without creating custom fields or formula logic. Bucketing lets an administrator define ranges of values for a field - such as the Contract Value currency field - and assign a label to each range, such as Small, Medium or Large (for example Small under $50,000 and Large over $200,000), all inside the report builder. It transforms raw values into meaningful categories for the report without touching the Account record or adding administrative overhead for new fields.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Group Rows) — merely clusters identical values together; it cannot turn a range of dollar values into a named size band.
Option B (Filter Logic) — decides which rows appear in the report; it does not label or categorise them.
Option C (Detail Column) — shows a field's raw value on each row; there is no categorisation without a bucket or a formula.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.reports_bucketing_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A Platform Administrator wants to limit the kinds of reports their users can create. Which tool should the administrator use?
explanation:
Hide Report Types is the tool. When users click New Report they are presented with a list of report types, which act as templates determining which objects and fields are available, and an org often has many standard report types that are irrelevant or confusing. The Select Report Types to Hide feature in Report and Dashboard Settings lets a Platform Administrator hide the unnecessary or redundant ones, so users only see the templates that align with company reporting standards, reducing the risk of inaccurate reports built on the wrong data model.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Report Folder Sharing) — controls who can view or edit existing reports; it does not restrict the creation of new ones from specific templates.
Option C (Standard Report Types) — these are the templates being limited, not a tool for limiting them; custom report types define what data is available, but the act of limiting the visible list is the hide feature.
Option D (Joined Report) — a report format for combining blocks from several report types; it does not restrict what users can create.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.reports_hide_report_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks has the organization wide defaults for Opportunity set to Private. Which two features should a Platform Administrator use to open up access to opportunity records for sales users working on collaborative deals?
explanation:
Sharing rules and the role hierarchy are the two features that open up access to opportunity records under a Private organization-wide default. Sharing rules grant lateral access to records based on criteria or ownership (for example, share all Large Deals with the Strategic Sales group). The role hierarchy automatically grants vertical access, so managers and users higher in the hierarchy can see and edit records owned by their subordinates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Sharing set) — a feature for Experience Cloud (community) users, granting them access to records related to their account; it is not used for standard internal sales users.
Option D (Profiles) — control what actions a user can perform (create, read, edit) but do not grant access to specific records the user does not own in a Private model.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks wants to leverage roll-up summaries on the Account object. Which standard object supports this roll-up summary natively?
explanation:
Opportunity is the standard object that supports roll-up summaries on Account natively. A roll-up summary field calculates values from related records and displays them on a master record, and it is available only on the master side of a master-detail relationship. For standard objects, Salesforce provides a built-in master-detail-like relationship between Account (master) and Opportunity (detail), so a Platform Administrator can create roll-up summary fields on the Account for the sum of opportunity amount, the minimum close date or a count of related opportunities.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Contact) — has a lookup relationship to Account rather than master-detail, so it does not support native roll-up summaries; rolling up contacts needs Flow or a third-party app.
Option C (Case) — the same: a lookup to Account, no native roll-up.
Option D (Campaigns) — does not share the required master-detail relationship with Account either.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_about_roll_up_summary_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5
