question: The administrator at AW Computing wants to send off client welcome tasks and a welcome email to the primary contact automatically when an Opportunity is Closed won. What automation tool best accomplishes this?
explanation:
Process Builder is the one automation tool among the options that can create a task and send an email off the back of a record change, so it is the exam answer. Build it in Flow, though: Salesforce ended support for Workflow Rules and Process Builder on 31 December 2025; existing automation still runs and can still be edited, but new work belongs in a record-triggered flow, which does both halves of this requirement - a Create Records element for the welcome task and an email action to the primary contact.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Validation Rule) — can only block a save; it creates nothing and sends nothing.
Option B (Outbound Message) — sends record data to an external endpoint; no task, no email to the contact.
Option C (Approval Process) — routes a record for sign-off; not a welcome-task or email mechanism.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000389396&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_concepts_trigger_record.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator has assigned a permission set group with the two-factor authentication for User Interface Logins permissions and the two-factor authentication for API Logins permission to a group of users. Which two prompts will happen when one of the users attempts to log in to Data Loader? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Users need to connect an authenticator app to their Salesforce account.
optionB: Users need to get a security token from a trusted network using Reset My Security Token.
optionC: Users need to download and install an authenticator app on theirmobile device.
optionD: Users need to enter a verification code from email or SMS, whichever has higher priority.
explanation:
Connecting an authenticator app to the Salesforce account, and downloading and installing an authenticator app on a mobile device, are the two prompts. Requiring multi-factor authentication for API logins means the Data Loader sign-in now needs a verification code, and a user who has no registered method is walked through enrolling one on that first attempt: install a TOTP authenticator app on a mobile device, then connect it to the Salesforce account by scanning the QR code or pasting the security key shown during enrolment.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (get a security token via Reset My Security Token) — a security token is a separate mechanism appended to the password for API access; it is emailed when reset rather than requested at login, so it is not one of the prompts.
Option D (enter a verification code from email or SMS) — codes delivered by email or SMS are not accepted as Salesforce MFA verification methods, so no such prompt appears.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.security_require_2fa_api.htm&type=5

corrected.note: Email and SMS codes are not valid Salesforce MFA verification methods, so the previously marked option cannot describe a real prompt. Enrolling a TOTP app is a two-step sequence — install the app, then connect it to the account — which is what the user is actually asked for.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters is using one profile for all of its marketing users, providing read-only access to the Campaign object. A few marketing users now require comprehensive edit access on Campaigns. How should an administrator fulfil this request?
explanation:
Permission sets are the answer, because a permission set grants extra access on top of whatever profile a user already has - exactly the shape of this problem, where most marketing users keep read-only access to Campaigns and a few need edit. The administrator builds one permission set with the campaign object permissions and assigns it to those few; nobody's profile changes and no second marketing profile has to be created and maintained in parallel.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Organization-wide defaults) — move the baseline for everyone, not for a few.
Option C (Marketing user checkbox) — a different control: it governs campaign management features such as creating campaigns and managing members, and would not grant object edit access on its own.
Option D (Field-level security) — governs individual fields, not the ability to edit the record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.perm_sets_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_object_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud kicks want to give credit to Opportunity team members based on the level of effort contributed by each person toward each deal. What feature should the administrator use to meet this requirement?
explanation:
Splits are the feature for dividing credit on a deal among the opportunity team. Each team member gets a share, and those shares roll into quota and pipeline reporting so the contribution is visible rather than anecdotal. There are two flavours worth telling apart: revenue splits divide the amount and must total 100 percent; overlay splits credit people who helped without owning the revenue - a sales engineer, for example - and are not constrained to total 100 percent.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Stages) — describe where a deal is; they allocate no credit.
Option C (Queues) — hold records awaiting an owner.
Option D (List Views) — only filter what you see.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.teamselling.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.salesteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters has requested that when the Referral Date field is updated on the custom object Referral Source, the parent object Referral also needs to be updated. Which automation solution should an administrator use to meet this request?
explanation:
Process Builder is the one option that can update a field on a parent record when a child changes, because it can traverse the relationship and write to the related record. As with the rest of this deck's Process Builder items, the exam answer stands but the modern build is a record-triggered flow on Referral Source with an Update Records element pointed at the parent - Salesforce ended support for Process Builder on 31 December 2025.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Lightning Web Component) — UI code, not automation; it would only act when someone opened the page.
Option B (Approval Process) — routes records for sign-off; it does not update a parent on a child change.
Option C (Workflow Field Update) — workflow can update a field on the record that triggered it, and on the master of a master-detail relationship, but not on an arbitrary parent.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_build_data_update.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000389396&language=en_US&type=1

question: Northern Trail outfitters has hired interns to enter Leads into Salesforce and has requested a way to is identify these new records from existing Leads. What approach should an administrator take to meet this requirement?
optionA: Set up Web-to-Lead form the interns use.
optionB: Define a record type and assign it to the interns.
optionC: Create a separate Lead Lightning App.
optionD: Update the active Leas Assignment Rules.
explanation:
Defining a record type and assigning it to the interns is the approach. A record type stamps each record with which process created it, and it is visible, filterable and reportable - so leads entered by the interns can be told apart from the rest simply by their record type, without inventing a custom field. Assigning that record type to the interns' profile (or via a permission set) means it is the one they get, while everyone else keeps the original.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a Web-to-Lead form for the interns) — Web-to-Lead creates leads from a form on a website, which is not what interns keying records into Salesforce are doing.
Option C (a separate Lead Lightning app) — changes navigation, not the data; the records would look the same.
Option D (update the active Lead Assignment Rules) — assignment rules decide who owns a lead once it exists; ownership is a poor proxy for who created it, since leads get reassigned.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.customize_recordtype.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_record_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Object Manager and Lightning App Builder

question: The Client services and customer support teams share the same profile but have different permission sets. The Custom Object Retention related list needs to be restricted to the client services teamon the Lightning record page layout. What should the administrator use to fulfil this request?
explanation:
Component Visibility is what restricts the Retention related list to the client services team. On a Lightning record page, a component's visibility can be conditioned on the viewing user's permissions - including a permission set the user holds - so the related list component is shown only to users with the client services permission set, even though both teams share one profile.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Sharing settings) — govern which records a user can see, not which components render on the page.
Option B (Page Layout Assignment) — layouts are assigned by profile and record type, and both teams share the same profile, so a layout cannot separate them.
Option D (Record Type Assignment) — record types are assigned by profile too, and would distinguish records rather than users.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_components_visibility.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator at Ursa Major Solar just learned about the AppExchange and how helpful it can be to the company's business. Which two actions can be accomplished via the AppExchange? Choose 2 answers.
explanation:
Finding certified developers and consultants, and installing industry-specific solution templates, are the two actions. AppExchange is a marketplace for two kinds of thing: software and people. On the software side it carries apps, components and industry solution templates that can be installed into an org. On the services side it lists certified consulting partners and developers who can be engaged for an implementation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (download the Data Loader tool) — Data Loader is downloaded from Setup, under Data Loader, not from AppExchange.
Option D (download standard Lightning components) — standard Lightning components ship with the platform and appear in Lightning App Builder already; what AppExchange offers is third-party components on top of those.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.dashboards_install_sample_appexchange.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.distribution_installing_packages.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator is building a Lightning app and sees a message that a My Domain must be set up first. What should the administrator take into consideration when enabling My Domain?
optionA: Single sign-on must be disabled prior toimplementing My Domain.
optionB: The login for all internal and external users changes to the My Domain login
optionC: A deployed My Domain is irreversible and renaming is unavailable.
optionD: The URL instance for a My Domain stays the same for every release
explanation:
The login for all internal and external users changing to the My Domain login is the consideration. My Domain replaces the org's instance URL with a branded one, and the consequence users feel immediately is the login URL: everyone signs in at the My Domain address instead of the generic login page, internal users and external users on Experience Cloud sites alike.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (single sign-on must be disabled first) — the opposite is true: My Domain is a prerequisite for several SSO and Lightning features.
Option C (a deployed My Domain is irreversible and cannot be renamed) — the name can be changed, and Salesforce documents how to manage redirections from the previous host name when you do.
Option D (the instance URL stays the same every release) — the instance behind an org can move between releases, which is one of the reasons to stop relying on instance URLs in the first place.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.domain_name_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.domain_name_setting_login_policy.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator at Ursa Major Solar needs to send information to an external accounting system. What workflow action should the administrator use to accomplish this?
explanation:
An Outbound Message is the workflow action built for sending data out of Salesforce. You define which fields to send and the endpoint URL to send them to, and Salesforce posts a SOAP message to that endpoint when the automation fires - which is exactly what handing information to an external accounting system means. It is declarative, so no Apex is involved, and Salesforce documents it as available to flows, workflow rules, approval processes and entitlement processes.
One currency note: since February 2026 outbound messages no longer carry a session id, so the receiving system authenticates with OAuth 2.0 rather than replaying a session from the payload.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Assign Task) — creates a task record for a user inside Salesforce; nothing leaves the org.
Option C (Create Record) — inserts a record of any object, again inside Salesforce.
Option D (Custom Notification) — pushes an in-app or mobile alert to Salesforce users, not data to an external system.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The sales manager at Cloud Kicks wants to set up a business process where opportunity discounts over 30% need to be approved by the VP of sales. Any discounts above 10% need to be approved by the user's manager. The administrator has been tasked with creating an approval process. Which are two considerations the administrator needs to review before setting up this approval process? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create a custom Discount field on the opportunity to capture the discount amount
optionB: Populate the Manager standard field on the sales users' User Detail page.
optionD: Allow the submitter choose the approver manually.
explanation:
Creating a custom Discount field on the opportunity and populating the Manager standard field on the sales users' records are the two prerequisites to review before the process can be built. Discount is not a standard field on Opportunity, so a custom field has to exist to hold the percentage that the entry criteria and steps will test. And routing a step to "the user's manager" uses the Manager field on the submitter's user record - if that field is empty the approval has nowhere to go. Salesforce's own Build a Discount Approval Process walkthrough sets up both before creating the process.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (configure two separate approval processes) — not required: a single process with conditional steps covers both tiers, routing anything over 10% to the manager and escalating over 30% to the VP.
Option D (let the submitter choose the approver manually) — would defeat the point of routing by discount size.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/projects/build-a-discount-approval-process/prepare-your-org

corrected.note: Routing to "the user's manager" only works if the Manager field on the user record is populated, which makes it a genuine prerequisite. Two separate approval processes are not one: a single process with conditional steps handles both the 10% and 30% tiers.

question: Cloud Kicks want its reports to show a Fiscal Year that starts on February 1 and has 12 months. How Should the Administrator Address this requirement?
optionA: Set the Fiscal Year to Custom and the starting month as February.
optionB: Set the Fiscal Year to Custom and the duration to 4 quarters.
optionC: Set the Fiscal Year to Standard and the starting month as February.
optionD: Set the Fiscal Year to Standard and the duration to 12 months.
explanation:
Setting the Fiscal Year to Standard with February as the starting month is the answer. Standard fiscal years in Salesforce follow the Gregorian calendar but may begin on the first day of any month, so a twelve-month year beginning 1 February is precisely a standard fiscal year with February chosen as the starting month.
Custom fiscal years exist for structures that do not map onto calendar months at all - 4-4-5 period layouts, 13-period years, or quarters built from a set number of weeks. Choosing Custom here would mean defining every period by hand to reproduce what the standard setting already provides, and once a custom fiscal year is enabled the feature cannot be turned back off.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Custom with February as the starting month) — Custom is for non-calendar structures; a February start is a standard fiscal year setting, and Custom is irreversible once enabled.
Option B (Custom with a duration of 4 quarters) — the same misuse of Custom, and "4 quarters" is not how a custom fiscal year is defined.
Option D (Standard with a duration of 12 months) — a standard fiscal year is always 12 months; there is no duration to set, and this option never chooses the February start the requirement needs.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.setting_the_fiscal_year.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: A standard fiscal year in Salesforce may begin on the first day of ANY month, so a 12-month year starting 1 February is exactly a standard fiscal year. Custom fiscal years exist for structures that do not follow calendar months (4-4-5, 13 periods). The explanation's claim that a standard year must start on January 1 is wrong.

question:
AW Computing would like to improve its Case Lightning record page by including:
* A filtered component to display a message in bold font when a case is saved as a critical record type.
* A quick way to update the account status from the case layout.
Which two components should an administrator use to satisfy these requests? Choose 2 answers.
explanation:
The Related Record component and the Rich Text component are the two standard Lightning page components, one per request. The Related Record component surfaces a related record's fields on this page and allows them to be edited in place - so an agent can update the account's status without leaving the case. It needs an update action to define which fields are editable. The Rich Text component holds formatted text, which is what makes the bold message possible; pair it with a component visibility filter on record type so it appears only on critical cases.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Related List) — shows child records rather than editable parent fields.
Option C (Record details) — shows the case's own fields, not the account's, and carries no formatted message.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.lightning_page_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_components_visibility.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Ursa Major Solar provides a 1-year warranty on all of the panels it installs. Installation details, along with the warranty information, a captured on a custom object called Installation. The installation record is created by the installer from the mobile app. Customers son receive a longer warranty as a way of increasing customer satisfaction when an installation gets delayed or has issues. How should the administrator configure Salesforce to capture the expiration date of the warranty?
optionA: Use a formula as the default value of the warranty Expiration Date field.
optionB: Create a formula field to display l year from the warranty purchased.
optionC: Add a validation rule to ensure the Expiration Date field is populated.
optionD: Include the warranty Expiration Date field on the mobile page layout.
explanation:
Using a formula as the default value of the Warranty Expiration Date field is the configuration. The requirement has two halves that pull in opposite directions: the date should normally be a year after installation, but it must be possible to give a customer a longer warranty. A default value formula does both - it calculates the usual date when the record is created, and leaves the field writable so anyone can override it afterwards.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a formula field showing one year from purchase) — a formula field cannot be overridden at all; it recalculates from its inputs every time it is read, so a goodwill extension would be impossible to record.
Option C (a validation rule requiring the Expiration Date) — only insists that the field is filled in; it never works out what the value should be.
Option D (add the field to the mobile page layout) — makes it visible to the installer but supplies no date, which just moves the typing onto the person in the field.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.fields_useful_default_field_values.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custom_field_attributes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator at Universal Containers has been asked to prevent users from accessing Salesforce from outside of their network. What are two considerations for this configuration? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: IP address restrictions are set on the profile or globally for the org.
optionB: Users can change their password to avoid login IP restrictions.
optionC: Enforce Login IP Ranges on Every Request must be selected to enforce IP restrictions.
optionD: Single sign-on will allow users to log in from anywhere.
explanation:
IP address restrictions being set on the profile or globally for the org, and Enforce Login IP Ranges on Every Request being required to enforce them fully, are the two considerations. IP address restrictions allow you to prevent users from accessing Salesforce from outside their network: they can be set on the profile (Login IP Ranges) or globally for the org (Network Access trusted ranges). By default a profile's login IP ranges are checked only at login; to enforce the restriction on every request, including API logins, you select Enforce Login IP Ranges on Every Request in Session Settings.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (users can change their password to avoid IP restrictions) — a password change has no bearing on where a login originates; the IP check is applied regardless of credentials.
Option D (single sign-on lets users log in from anywhere) — login IP ranges on the profile still apply to SSO users, so SSO is not a bypass.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_networkaccess.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.login_ip_ranges.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Users at Cloud Kicks want to be able to create a task that will repeat every two weeks. What should an administrator do to meet the requirement?
optionC: Workflow rule to create recurring tasks.
explanation:
Enabling Creation of Recurring Tasks is what the administrator does, because recurring tasks are switched on at org level, not per user. Enable Recurring Tasks in Lightning Experience and the Salesforce Mobile App gives the path: from Setup, find Activity Settings, select Enable Creation of Recurring Tasks, and save. After that, add the Create Recurring Series of Tasks field to the task page layouts so users can actually set a recurrence - here, every two weeks.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a flow to create recurring tasks) — could manufacture a series of separate task records, but they would be unrelated tasks rather than a recurring series, with no series to view or delete as a unit.
Option C (a workflow rule to create recurring tasks) — the same problem, in a tool that is now past end of support.
Option D (Turn on Recurring Activities) — there is no setting by that name.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.tasks_enable_recurring_tasks_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: The explanation said the permission to create recurring tasks is enabled by administrators in the user profile settings. It is not a profile permission - Enable Creation of Recurring Tasks is an org-level checkbox in Activity Settings, and the page layout needs the Create Recurring Series of Tasks field before users can use it.

question: The business development team at Cloud Kicks thinks the account creation process has too many fields to fill out and the page feels cluttered. They have requested the administrator to simplify the process. Which automation tool should an administrator use?
explanation:
Flow Builder is the tool, because the complaint is about the shape of the data-entry experience and a screen flow is the only option here that can change it. Flow Builder can present a short, ordered sequence of screens asking for just the fields that matter, branch on what the user answers, and create the account at the end - so the clutter of a full page layout never appears.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Approval process) — routes a record for sign-off after it exists; it builds no user interface.
Option B (Workflow rule) — acts after a save and cannot collect input.
Option D (Validation rule) — can only reject a save, which makes data entry more frustrating rather than less.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_forms_with_screen_flow_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters has a custom quick action on Account that creates a new Case. How should an administrator make the quick action available on the Salesforce mobile app?
optionA: Create a custom Lightning App with the action.
optionB: Modify compact Case page layout to include the action.
optionC: Include the action in the Salesforce Mobile Navigation menu.
optionD: Add the Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience action to the page layout.
explanation:
Adding the action to the Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions section of the page layout is how to make the quick action available in the mobile app. That section of the Account page layout controls which actions appear on the record in both Lightning Experience and the mobile app; in the page layout editor you drag the Create Case quick action into it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom Lightning app with the action) — apps hold tabs and navigation, not record-level quick actions.
Option B (the compact Case page layout) — compact layouts pick the fields shown in the highlights panel and mobile record header; they do not hold actions, and the action lives on Account anyway.
Option C (the Salesforce Mobile Navigation menu) — the navigation menu lists tabs and pages, not quick actions on a record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.adding_actions_using_ple.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks users are seeing error messages when they use one of their screen flows. The error messages are confusing but could be resolved if the users entered more information on the account before starting the flow. How should the administrator address this issues?
optionA: Remove validation rules so that the users are able to process without complete records.
optionB: Create a permission set to allow users to bypass the error.
optionC: use a fault connector and display a screen with text explaining what went wrong and how to correct it.
optionD: Uncheck the end user Flow Errors box in setup.
explanation:
Using a fault connector and displaying a screen with text explaining what went wrong and how to correct it is the right fix. The users are not hitting a bug - they are hitting a real failure with an unhelpful message. A fault connector is how a flow catches that: drag the fault path off the element that fails and route it to a screen whose display text explains, in the org's own words, what is missing and how to fix it. That leaves the underlying rules intact.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (remove the validation rules) — lets incomplete accounts save; it removes the protection rather than explaining it.
Option B (a permission set to bypass the error) — does the same for a subset of users.
Option D (uncheck the end-user flow errors box) — suppressing flow error emails hides the problem from the administrator without changing anything the user sees.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.flow_ref_elements.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_forms_with_screen_flow_components.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The administrator at cloud kicks is trying to debug a screen flow that create contacts. One of the variables in the flow is missing on the debug screen. What could cause this issue?
optionA: The available for input checkbox was unchecked.
optionB: The flow is an inactive version
optionC: The field type is unsupported by debugging.
optionD: The available for output checkbox was unchecked.
explanation:
The Available for input checkbox being unchecked is the cause. The debug window offers a value for a variable only when that variable can be set from outside the flow, and that is what Available for input controls. Clear the checkbox and the variable still exists and still works inside the flow - it simply stops accepting a value from a caller, a URL parameter, or the debug screen, so it disappears from the list of inputs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the flow is an inactive version) — debugging runs against a specific version rather than requiring an active one.
Option C (the field type is unsupported by debugging) — there is no field type that debug refuses to show.
Option D (the Available for output checkbox was unchecked) — the mirror image: it governs whether the value can be read by whatever called the flow, and has no effect on what debug asks for.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_considerations_feature_variable.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Users at Cloud Kicks are reporting different options when uploading a custom picklist on the Opportunity object based on the kind of opportunity. Where Should an administrator update the option in the picklist?
explanation:
Record Type is where the administrator updates the picklist options. Record types are what vary a picklist's available values by the kind of opportunity: Edit Picklists for Record Types and Business Processes describes selecting the record type and editing the picklist field to change which values it offers. Users seeing different options on the same field are seeing different record types, so that is where the change belongs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Fields and relationships) — edits the field's master value list for every record; it cannot vary the options by kind of opportunity.
Option B (Related lookup filters) — restrict which records a lookup field accepts; they have nothing to do with picklist values.
Option D (Picklist value sets) — a global value set defines one shared list of values across fields; the per-record-type selection is still made on the record type.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.customize_recordtype.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.customize_recordtype.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.editing_picklists_for_record_types_and_business_processes.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator has been asked to update a flow that was created as part of a recent update. When the administrator opens the flow for editing, the Flow toolbox offers only four elements: Assignment, Decision, Get Records, and Loop. What would cause this?
optionA: The flow is a screen flow.
optionB: The version of the flow is inactive.
optionC: The flow is a before save flow.
optionD: The version of the flow is activated.
explanation:
The flow being a before-save flow is what causes the short toolbox. A before-save record-triggered flow runs inside the save itself, before the record is written, and that is why its toolbox is so short: Assignment, Decision, Get Records, and Loop. It can read data and work out values, then set fields on the triggering record through $Record - but it cannot create, update or delete anything, call an action, or show a screen.
That restriction is the price of the speed. Because the flow writes to the record already in memory, there is no second save, which is what makes before-save flows dramatically faster than the after-save equivalent for same-record field updates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the flow is a screen flow) — a screen flow is not record-triggered at all, and it offers the Screen element among many others.
Option B (the version is inactive) — whether a version is active or inactive changes nothing about which elements are offered.
Option D (the version is activated) — the same: activation state does not shape the toolbox.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.flow_ref_elements.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_concepts_trigger_record.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.flow_ref_elements.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: When a cloud kicks Opportunity closes, the company would like to automatically create a renewal opportunity. Which automation tool should an administrator use to accomplish this request?
explanation:
Flow Builder is the tool, because creating a renewal opportunity means inserting a record and Flow Builder is the only option offered here that can do that: a record-triggered flow fires when the opportunity closes, and a Create Records element builds the renewal from the closing deal.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Approval Process) — routes an existing record for sign-off; it does not produce a new opportunity.
Option C (Opportunity sharing rule) — governs who can see a record, nothing more.
Option D (Validation rule) — only blocks a save when a condition fails; it can never create anything.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.flow_considerations_trigger_record.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.flow_considerations_trigger_record.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: A validation rule cannot create a record, so it can never be half of the answer here. The explanation argues for "Flow Builder and Process Builder", but Process Builder is not among the options — the source lost it. Only Flow Builder is defensible, so the item is now a single-answer question rather than a "choose 2" with one impossible half.

question: Cloud Kicks needs to change the owner of a case when it has been open for more than 7 days. How should the administrator complete this requirement?
explanation:
An Escalation Rule is the only tool here that measures elapsed time. An escalation rule entry ages a case from its creation date, and when the case passes the threshold - seven days in this scenario - its escalation actions run. Reassigning the case to another user or a queue is one of the two things those actions can do; sending notification email is the other.
One configuration detail that trips people up: escalation ages are counted against business hours, so a rule intended to fire after seven calendar days needs business hours that run around the clock.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Auto-Response Rules) — reply to the customer and change nothing about ownership.
Option B (Validation Rule) — can only block a save.
Option D (Assignment Rule) — fires when a case is created or reassigned, so it cannot notice that a week has gone by.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.rules_escalation_actions.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.customize_supporthours.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which three items are available in the mobile navigation menu? Choose 3 answers.
explanation:
Lightning App Pages, Chatter and Dashboards are the three menu items. The mobile navigation menu is built from things that behave like tabs. Anything represented by a tab is eligible - standard and custom objects, the Chatter feed, People and Groups - and to that Salesforce adds Lightning app pages, Visualforce pages and a set of productivity items, Dashboards among them. What each user actually sees is still filtered by their profile's tab settings.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Lightning Home Page) — the landing page of a Lightning app rather than an entry in the menu.
Option D (Utility Bar) — a docked strip along the bottom of a desktop Lightning app; it does not exist in the mobile app at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.salesforce_app_customize_nav_menu.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has two sales teams, Sales team A and Sales team B. Each team has their own role in the role hierarchy. Both roles are subordinates of the same Manager role. How should the administrator share records owned by sales team A with Sales team B?
explanation:
Owner-based sharing is how to do it: an owner-based sharing rule shares records according to who owns them, so set it to share the records owned by the Sales Team A role with the Sales Team B role, and every current and future record follows automatically.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Hierarchical sharing) — the role hierarchy only grants access upward, which is why the shared Manager role can see both teams' records while the two peer roles still cannot see each other's.
Option B (Manual sharing) — grants access one record at a time and is performed by the record owner, so it neither scales to a whole team nor is something an administrator configures centrally.
Option C (Criteria based sharing) — keys off field values on the record rather than off its owner, so it does not express "owned by Sales Team A".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&type=5&language=en_US
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Sharing the records owned by one role with another peer role is the textbook use of an owner-based sharing rule. Manual sharing is a per-record action taken by the owner, not something an administrator configures for a whole team.

question: Which tool should an administrator use to identify and fix potential session vulnerabilities?
explanation:
Security Health Check is the page built for identifying and fixing session vulnerabilities. It reads the org's security settings, compares them against a baseline - the Salesforce Baseline Standard, or one of up to five custom baselines you upload - and reports a score with the settings that fall short grouped as High, Medium, Low risk or Informational. Session settings are among the settings it grades. The part that answers "and fix" is Fix Risks, which resets the flagged settings to the baseline's recommended values without leaving the page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Field History Tracking) — records changes to record data; it says nothing about security settings.
Option B (Setup Audit Trail) — lists configuration changes after the fact; it neither grades settings nor fixes them.
Option D (Organization-Wide Defaults) — one of the settings Health Check grades rather than a tool for finding weak ones.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_health_check.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator at Dreamhouse Reality needs to create customized pages for the Salesforce mobile app. Which two types of pages could an administrator build and customize using the Lightning App Builder? Choose 2 answers.
explanation:
App page and Record Page are the two types. Lightning App Builder builds App pages, Home pages, Record pages and Email Application panes. The two that matter for the Salesforce mobile app are the App page - a custom page of components that appears as an item in the mobile navigation menu - and the Record page, which lays out an individual record for viewing and editing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (User Page) — there is no User page type in App Builder.
Option B (Dashboard page) — no such page type either; dashboards are built in the Reports and Dashboards tools and can only be surfaced on a Lightning page as a component.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=platform.lightning_page_types.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.lightning_page_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Object Manager and Lightning App Builder

corrected.note: The explanation states outright that App page and Record page are the App Builder page types and that User page and Dashboard page are not — while the answer key marked the latter two.

question: What is the order of execution when a Case record is saved?
optionA: Validation rules, Escalation rules, Workflow rules, Auto-response rules
optionB: Assignment rules, Auto-response rules, Workflow rules, Escalation rules
optionC: Assignment rules, Validation rules, Workflow rules, Escalation rules
optionD: Validation rules, Assignment rules, Escalation rules, Auto-response rules
explanation:
Assignment rules, then auto-response rules, then workflow rules, then escalation rules is the order. The Apex Developer Guide sets out the save order, and for a Case the four rules in these options run in this sequence: after triggers, then assignment rules, then auto-response rules, then workflow rules, and - after the workflow field updates and their re-validation - escalation rules.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (validation, escalation, workflow, auto-response) — validation runs well before any of the four, as part of the system validation steps that precede the save, and escalation rules run last of the four, not second.
Option C (assignment, validation, workflow, escalation) — validation does not sit between assignment and workflow; it has already run before the record is saved.
Option D (validation, assignment, escalation, auto-response) — escalation is evaluated after the record has been written and after workflow has had its turn, so it cannot precede auto-response rules.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm

question: The administrator has been asked to automate a simple field update on the account. When a support agent changes the status of the account to 'Audited', they would like the system to automatically update the Audited date field on the account with today's date. Which tool should the administrator use to complete this automation?
explanation:
Flow Builder is the tool. Recording the date a status changed means writing a value into the Audited Date field, and a record-triggered flow on Account does exactly that: when Status becomes "Audited", an Update Records element stamps the date into the field, where it then stays.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Approval process) — routes a record for sign-off; it does not react to a status change by writing a date.
Option B (Formula Field) — fails for two separate reasons: it is read-only and computes a value for display rather than storing one, so it cannot populate a different field; and a formula returning TODAY() re-evaluates every day, so it would always show the current date rather than the day the account was audited.
Option D (Validation Rule) — can only block a save; it writes nothing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_build_data_update.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: A formula field is read-only and cannot write a value into another field. It would also give the wrong result: TODAY() re-evaluates every day, so the stamp would drift instead of recording when the status changed. Writing a date on a field change needs Flow Builder.

question: Universal Containers administrator has been asked to create a many-to-many relationship between two existing custom objects. Which two steps should the administrator take when enabling the many-to-many relationship? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create a junction with a custom object.
optionB: Create two master detail relationships on the new object.
optionC: Create two lookup relationships on the new object.
optionD: Create URL fields on a custom object.
explanation:
Creating a junction with a custom object and giving it two master-detail relationships are the two steps. Salesforce has no many-to-many relationship type, so you build one out of parts: create a custom object to sit between the two - the junction object - and give it two master-detail relationships, one to each side. The order matters in practice: the first master-detail you create becomes the primary relationship, which determines the junction record's look and feel, its owner, and which parent's sharing it inherits.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (two lookup relationships on the new object) — would technically link the objects but give up what master-detail provides here: required parents, so no junction record can be orphaned, cascade delete when a parent goes, and roll-up summaries on either side.
Option D (URL fields on a custom object) — link to web addresses and create no relationship at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.relationships_manytomany.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.overview_of_custom_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Object Manager and Lightning App Builder

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has deployed my domain. The Chief Marketing Officer wants to make sure that all of the Salesforce users log in using the branded login URL. There needs to be a grace period for the user's bookmarks to be updated. How should the administrator configure the policies in my domain settings?
optionA: Set the login policy to require login from https://nto.my.salesforce.com
optionB: Set the Redirect policy to Do Not redirect.
optionC: Set the redirect policy to Redirect with a warning to the same page within the domain.
optionD: Set the login policy to prevent login from https://login.salesforce.com
explanation:
Setting the redirect policy to Redirect with a warning to the same page within the domain is the configuration. The requirement contains its own answer: users must end up on the branded URL, but there has to be a grace period while bookmarks are updated. Redirecting with a warning does both - the user still arrives where they were going, and sees a message telling them the address has changed. The usual sequence is to redirect with a warning first, and tighten the login policy once traffic on the old URLs has died away.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (login policy requiring login from the My Domain URL) — the opposite of a grace period: it cuts off anyone still using an old bookmark immediately, which is the right end state but the wrong first step.
Option B (redirect policy set to Do Not redirect) — leaves the old URLs working silently, so nobody ever updates a bookmark.
Option D (login policy preventing login from login.salesforce.com) — the same immediate cut-off as A, with no warning to move bookmarks.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.domain_name_setting_login_policy.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.domain_name_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Cloud Kicks (CK) stores information about specific customers in Contacts and information about shoes and accessories in a custom Merchandise object. What should the CK administrator use to represent that Contact can be interested in multiple pieces of Merchandies?
explanation:
A Junction object is what represents a Contact being interested in multiple pieces of Merchandise. A junction object is a custom object that creates a many-to-many relationship between two other objects: each record of one object can be related to multiple records of the other, and vice versa - a contact interested in many pieces of merchandise, and a piece of merchandise of interest to many contacts. The junction object carries two master-detail relationships, one to each of the objects it connects.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Hierarchy column) — not a relationship feature; nothing by that name links two objects many-to-many.
Option B (Lookup filter) — restricts which records a lookup field will accept; it cannot make one contact relate to many merchandise records.
Option C (Formula field) — computes a value for display and creates no relationship.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.relationships_manytomany.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.relationships_manytomany.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Object Manager and Lightning App Builder

question: An administrator installed a managed package that contains a permission set group. The permission set group that was installed includes Delete access on several objects, and the administrator needs to prevent users in the permission set group from being able to delete records. What should the administrator do to control Delete access?
optionA: Use a muting permission set with a permission set group to mute selected permissions.
optionB: Create a new permission set that has Delete access deselected for the objects.
optionC: Create a new role that prevents Delete permissions from rolling up to the users.
optionD: Edit the profile for the users to remove Delete access from the objects.
explanation:
Using a muting permission set within the permission set group to mute the selected permissions is what controls Delete access. The permission set group came from a managed package, so its permission sets cannot be edited. A muting permission set is the mechanism designed for exactly that: it sits inside the group and disables selected permissions the group would otherwise grant, without touching the packaged permission sets themselves. Users assigned to that group lose Delete; anyone assigned one of those permission sets directly, outside the group, is unaffected.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a new permission set with Delete deselected) — permissions are additive, and deselecting an access in one permission set never takes away what another grants.
Option C (a new role to stop Delete rolling up) — roles govern record visibility, not object permissions.

question: An administration needs to store the ID of record type of later use in a flow. Which kind of variable should the administrator use?
explanation:
A Text variable is the kind to use. Flow variable data types are Text, Number, Currency, Boolean, Date, Date/Time, Picklist, Multi-Select Picklist, Record and Apex-Defined. There is no ID type, so a record type id - an 18-character string - is held in a Text variable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Boolean variable) — holds only true or false.
Option C (ID variable) — no such flow variable type exists.
Option D (Record variable) — stores a whole record and its fields rather than a single id value.

question: An administrator at Northern Trail Outfitters is unable to add a new user in salesforce. What could cause this issue?
optionA: The Username is not a corporate email address
optionB: The username is less than 80 characters.
optionC: The Username is a fake email address.
optionD: The Username is already in use.
explanation:
The username already being in use is the usual cause. A Salesforce username has to be unique across every Salesforce org in existence - production, sandbox and trial alike - so the usual reason a new user will not save is that the username has already been taken somewhere. The practical workaround is to keep the person's real email in the Email field and give the username a suffix that makes it globally unique.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the username is not a corporate email address) — a username must look like an email address, but it does not have to belong to the company's domain.
Option B (the username is less than 80 characters) — 80 characters is the maximum, so being under it is a requirement met rather than a problem.
Option C (the username is a fake email address) — it does not have to be a working address, so a fictitious one does not block the save.
